Embedded AI · Computer Vision · Edge Deployment

From Hand Gestures to Embedded AI: Building a Real-Time Drawing Interface

How a custom YOLOv8 segmentation model became a gesture-controlled drawing application on NVIDIA Jetson — and what deployment taught us about data quality and performance.

Technical project · ESIEE Paris · 2025–2026 · Anaïs Sallard & Erwin Dumontel

Could a camera replace a mouse or touchscreen for a simple drawing task? We built a contactless interface in which hand gestures control a virtual pen, then moved the application from a development PC to an embedded NVIDIA Jetson platform. The challenge was not just to train a neural network: it was to make the entire camera-to-action pipeline usable.

Designing the interaction

We defined four gestures: Draw (index finger extended), Save (V sign), Pause (open palm), and Delete (closed fist). We selected instance segmentation rather than bounding-box detection because the contour of the hand could also be used to locate the virtual pen.

The dataset was the first engineering challenge

Using Roboflow, we annotated hand masks and built a dataset covering different distances, lighting conditions, backgrounds and hands appearing in front of faces. One annotation failure was particularly revealing: the segmentation tool initially included part of a face with the hand. We corrected these masks manually.

Engineering lesson
A nearly perfect confusion matrix on a small validation split is not proof of robust performance in front of a live camera. Earlier dataset versions scored well on familiar images but struggled in the actual interaction setting.

The report documents iterative dataset refinement, including augmentation and several training runs. The selected configuration used a YOLOv8 nano segmentation model, 224 × 224 input images, a batch size of 64, and 100 epochs. Longer training and stronger augmentation did not consistently improve the confusion matrix, so we retained the earlier configuration for integration.

Turning segmentation into a drawing tool

For each video frame, the application obtains the segmentation contour and selects the point with the smallest vertical image coordinate as an approximate fingertip. Consecutive fingertip positions are connected to draw a line. This lightweight geometric heuristic avoids a separate landmark detector, although it assumes a suitable hand orientation.

Fingertip heuristic — image-coordinate geometry
ptip = arg minp ∈ contour y(p)
Because image y-coordinates increase downward, the topmost contour point is the minimum-y point. It is a practical approximation, not a general-purpose fingertip detector.

The PC application displayed the annotated camera feed and a separate drawing window. On Jetson, we reduced display overhead by using a single view. The report also discusses multi-hand action arbitration, but its implementation was not completed and is not presented here as a tested feature.

Measuring the embedded performance

We compared the PyTorch .pt model against a TensorRT .engine export, then tested GStreamer-based camera acquisition. Each configuration was measured over approximately 300 frames.

7.77FPS · PyTorch + OpenCV
8.29FPS · TensorRT + OpenCV
9.02FPS · TensorRT + GStreamer
Throughput gain — relative change
Gain = (FPSnew − FPSbase) / FPSbase × 100%
(9.02 − 7.77) / 7.77 × 100 ≈ 16.1%
The reported mean per-frame inference timing also fell from 37.49 ms to 27.06 ms. FPS and inference timing measure different portions of the pipeline and should not be treated as reciprocal quantities.

The improvement was meaningful for this prototype, but 9 FPS is still below a conventional 30 FPS video target. The work demonstrates optimization and deployment, not a claim of fully smooth high-frame-rate interaction.

What the project demonstrated

This project connected data annotation, model training, Python/OpenCV application design, segmentation-based interaction and GPU-accelerated deployment. Its most valuable result was learning to evaluate the whole system: a good offline metric can hide live-camera errors, and a faster model does not automatically remove camera and display bottlenecks.

The final prototype remained imperfect — including occasional background misclassifications — but it provided a working foundation and measurable evidence that TensorRT and a different capture pipeline improved embedded throughput.

Tools: Roboflow · YOLOv8-seg · Google Colab · Python · OpenCV · TensorRT · GStreamer · NVIDIA Jetson
